claim: Indirect neurogenesis by outer subventricular zone (OSVZ) neural stem cells drives the evolution of lissencephalic brains to gyrencephalic brains in vertebrates.
source: Indirect neurogenesis by the outer subventricular zone (OSVZ) neural stem cells drives the evolution of lissencephalic brains to gyrencephalic brains in vertebrates (Cárdenas and Borrell, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cárdenas and Borrell, 2020.

claim: Loss of function of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) did not lead to intermediate progenitors reverting into neural stem cells.
source: However, loss of function of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) did not lead to intermediate progenitors reverting into neural stem cells (Abdusselamoglu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Abdusselamoglu et al., 2019.

claim: Type II neuroblasts undergo indirect neurogenesis, similar to OSVZ neural stem cells.
source: By contrast, type II neuroblasts undergo indirect neurogenesis, similar to OSVZ neural stem cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge about type II neuroblasts and comparison to OSVZ neural stem cells.

claim: Type II neuroblasts continually undergo asymmetric division to self-renew and to generate a sibling cell that commits to an intermediate progenitor (INP) identity.
source: Type II neuroblasts continually undergo asymmetric division to self-renew and to generate a sibling cell that commits to an intermediate progenitor (INP) identity (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008.

claim: Buttonhead (Btd) and PointedP1 (PntP1) are specifically expressed in type II neuroblasts.
source: The Sp family transcription factor Buttonhead (Btd) and the ETS-1 transcription factor PointedP1 (PntP1) are specifically expressed in type II neuroblasts (Komori et al., 2014b; Xie et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Komori et al., 2014b; Xie et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2011.

claim: Btd and PntP1 expression levels decrease as a newly generated immature INP transitions into a non-Asense-expressing (Ase-) immature INP.
source: Btd and PntP1 expression levels decrease as a newly generated immature INP transitions into a non-Asense-expressing (Ase-) immature INP.
evidence: The claim is based on observations described in the manuscript about expression patterns during INP commitment.

claim: Three to four hrs after the transition to Ase- immature INP, an Ase- immature INP upregulates Ase expression as it progresses through INP commitment.
source: Three to four hrs after this transition, an Ase- immature INP upregulates Ase expression as it progresses through INP commitment.
evidence: The claim describes temporal dynamics of Ase expression during INP commitment based on established knowledge.

claim: Once INP commitment is complete, an Ase+ immature INP transitions into an INP that undergoes six to eight rounds of asymmetric division.
source: Once INP commitment is complete, an Ase+ immature INP transitions into an INP that undergoes six to eight rounds of asymmetric division.
evidence: The claim describes the behavior of INPs after commitment based on established knowledge.

claim: Notch signaling maintains type II neuroblasts in an undifferentiated state, partially by poising transcription of the master regulator of differentiation earmuff (erm).
source: Notch signaling maintains type II neuroblasts in an undifferentiated state, partially by poising transcription of the master regulator of differentiation earmuff (erm) (Janssens et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Janssens et al., 2017.

claim: During asymmetric neuroblast division, the TRIM-NHL protein Brain tumor (Brat) segregates into the newly generated immature INP and targets transcripts encoded by Notch downstream effector genes for RNA decay.
source: During asymmetric neuroblast division, the TRIM-NHL protein Brain tumor (Brat) segregates into the newly generated immature INP and targets transcripts encoded by Notch downstream effector genes for RNA decay (Bello et al., 2006; Betschinger et al., 2006; Komori et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2006b; Xiao et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bello et al., 2006; Betschinger et al., 2006; Komori et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2006b; Xiao et al., 2012.

claim: brat-null brains accumulate thousands of supernumerary type II neuroblasts that originate from the reversion of newly generated immature INPs due to defects in the downregulation of Notch signaling.
source: brat-null brains accumulate thousands of supernumerary type II neuroblasts that originate from the reversion of newly generated immature INPs due to defects in the downregulation of Notch signaling (Komori et al., 2014a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Komori et al., 2014a.

claim: The nuclear protein Insensible (Insb) inhibits the activity of Notch downstream effector proteins during asymmetric neuroblast division.
source: In parallel to Brat, the nuclear protein Insensible (Insb) inhibits the activity of Notch downstream effector proteins during asymmetric neuroblast division, and Insb overexpression efficiently triggers premature differentiation in type II neuroblasts (Komori et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Komori et al., 2018.

claim: Insb overexpression efficiently triggers premature differentiation in type II neuroblasts.
source: In parallel to Brat, the nuclear protein Insensible (Insb) inhibits the activity of Notch downstream effector proteins during asymmetric neuroblast division, and Insb overexpression efficiently triggers premature differentiation in type II neuroblasts (Komori et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Komori et al., 2018.

claim: Erm expression is maintained in immature INPs but becomes downregulated in INPs.
source: Erm expression is maintained in immature INPs but becomes downregulated in INPs (Janssens et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Janssens et al., 2014.

claim: Erm belongs to a family of transcription factors that are highly expressed in neural progenitors and can bind histone deacetylase 3 (Hdac3).
source: Erm belongs to a family of transcription factors that are highly expressed in neural progenitors and can bind histone deacetylase 3 (Hdac3) (Hirata et al., 2006; Koe et al., 2014; Levkowitz et al., 2003; Weng et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hirata et al., 2006; Koe et al., 2014; Levkowitz et al., 2003; Weng et al., 2010.

claim: Erm prevents INP reversion by repressing gene transcription.
source: Erm prevents INP reversion by repressing gene transcription.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Erm function.

claim: In erm-null brains, INPs spontaneously revert to type II neuroblasts.
source: In erm-null brains, INPs spontaneously revert to type II neuroblasts; however, this phenotype can be suppressed by knocking-down Notch function (Weng et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Weng et al., 2010.

claim: The INP reversion phenotype in erm-null brains can be suppressed by knocking-down Notch function.
source: In erm-null brains, INPs spontaneously revert to type II neuroblasts; however, this phenotype can be suppressed by knocking-down Notch function (Weng et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Weng et al., 2010.

claim: tailless (tll) was identified as a master regulator of type II neuroblast functional identity by comparing mRNAs enriched in type II neuroblasts or immature INPs.
source: By comparing mRNAs enriched in type II neuroblasts or immature INPs, we identified tailless (tll) as a master regulator of type II neuroblast functional identity.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA sequencing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tll is expressed in type II neuroblasts but not in INPs.
source: Tll is expressed in type II neuroblasts but not in INPs; moreover, Tll is necessary and sufficient for type II neuroblast functionality.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 1H and related text.

claim: Tll is necessary and sufficient for type II neuroblast functionality.
source: Tll is expressed in type II neuroblasts but not in INPs; moreover, Tll is necessary and sufficient for type II neuroblast functionality.
evidence: The claim is supported by loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Tll overexpression is sufficient to transform type I neuroblasts into type II neuroblasts.
source: Tll overexpression is sufficient to transform type I neuroblasts into type II neuroblasts, as indicated by changes in gene expression and an acquired competence for generating INPs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and related text.

claim: hamlet (ham) was identified as a new negative regulator of type II neuroblast maintenance.
source: We identified hamlet (ham) as a new negative regulator of type II neuroblast maintenance.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: ham is expressed after erm in immature INP during INP commitment.
source: ham is expressed after erm in immature INP during INP commitment, and Erm and Ham function through Hdac3 to continually inactivate tll.
evidence: The claim is based on expression analysis and temporal data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Erm and Ham function through Hdac3 to continually inactivate tll.
source: ham is expressed after erm in immature INP during INP commitment, and Erm and Ham function through Hdac3 to continually inactivate tll.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction experiments and knockdown studies described in the manuscript.

claim: Sequential inactivation during INP commitment suppresses tll activation by Notch signaling in INPs.
source: Sequential inactivation during INP commitment suppresses tll activation by Notch signaling in INPs.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic experiments showing the relationship between Erm, Ham, and Notch signaling.

claim: Overexpressing Insb for 6 hr did not significantly affect the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in brat-null brains.
source: Overexpressing Insb for 6 hr did not significantly affect the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in brat-null brains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 12 or more hours of Insb overexpression led to a time-dependent decrease in supernumerary type II neuroblasts and a corresponding increase in INPs.
source: By contrast, 12 or more hours of Insb overexpression led to a time-dependent decrease in supernumerary type II neuroblasts and a corresponding increase in INPs.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Transient Insb overexpression can induce supernumerary type II neuroblasts to synchronously transition into INPs in brat-null brains.
source: These results demonstrate that transient Insb overexpression can induce supernumerary type II neuroblasts to synchronously transition into INPs in brat-null brains.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental results showing synchronized INP commitment upon Insb overexpression.

claim: pntP1 mRNA levels increased within the first 6 hr of Insb overexpression, and then continually declined.
source: We found that pntP1 mRNA levels increased within the first 6 hr of Insb overexpression, and then continually declined (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: erm transcription rapidly increased in the first 12 hr of Insb overexpression, plateauing between 12 and 18 hr.
source: By contrast, erm transcription rapidly increased in the first 12 hr of Insb overexpression, plateauing between 12 and 18 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ase transcription showed little change in the first 6 hr of Insb overexpression, and then steadily increased between 12 and 24 hr.
source: ase transcription showed little change in the first 6 hr of Insb overexpression, and then steadily increased between 12 and 24 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Type II neuroblasts transiently overexpressing Insb for 6 hr in brat-null brains are at an equivalent stage as a newly generated immature INP transitioning to an Ase- immature INP in wild-type brains.
source: The combined temporal patterns of pntP1, erm, and ase transcription strongly suggest that type II neuroblasts transiently overexpressing Insb for 6 hr in brat-null brains are at an equivalent stage as a newly generated immature INP transitioning to an Ase- immature INP in wild-type brains.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from temporal gene expression patterns.

claim: Following 9 hr of Insb overexpression most type II neuroblasts in brat-null brains expressed cell identity markers indicative of Ase- immature INPs (Erm::V5+Ase-).
source: Indeed, following 9 hr of Insb overexpression most type II neuroblasts in brat-null brains expressed cell identity markers indicative of Ase- immature INPs (Erm::V5+Ase-), whereas after 18 hr of Insb overexpression they expressed markers indicative of Ase+ immature INPs (Erm::V5+Ase+) (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C-F.

claim: After 18 hr of Insb overexpression type II neuroblasts in brat-null brains expressed markers indicative of Ase+ immature INPs (Erm::V5+Ase+).
source: Indeed, following 9 hr of Insb overexpression most type II neuroblasts in brat-null brains expressed cell identity markers indicative of Ase- immature INPs (Erm::V5+Ase-), whereas after 18 hr of Insb overexpression they expressed markers indicative of Ase+ immature INPs (Erm::V5+Ase+) (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C-F.

claim: 76 genes were reproducibly downregulated by 1.5-fold or more in brat-null brains overexpressing Insb for 9 hr.
source: By sequencing mRNA in triplicate following the transient over-expression strategy (Figure 1C), we identified 76 genes that were reproducibly downregulated by 1.5-fold or more in brat-null brains overexpressing Insb for 9 hr (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: tll was the most downregulated gene in brat-null brains overexpressing Insb for 9 hr.
source: Of these genes, tll was the most downregulated; similarly, tll was the most downregulated gene in brat-null brains overexpressing Insb for 18 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: tll was the most downregulated gene in brat-null brains overexpressing Insb for 18 hr.
source: Of these genes, tll was the most downregulated; similarly, tll was the most downregulated gene in brat-null brains overexpressing Insb for 18 hr.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Tll::GFP is detected in type II neuroblasts but not in immature or mature INPs.
source: Consistent with previous study (Bayraktar and Doe, 2013), we detected Tll::GFP in type II neuroblasts but not in immature or mature INPs (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1H and citation to Bayraktar and Doe, 2013.

claim: Tll::GFP expression is detected in type I neuroblasts in the brain and in the ventral nerve cord, but at a significantly lower level than in type II neuroblasts.
source: Tll::GFP expression is also detected in type I neuroblasts in the brain and in the ventral nerve cord, but at a significantly lower level than in type II neuroblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-E.

claim: Control brains always contained eight type II neuroblasts per lobe.
source: Whereas control brains always contained eight type II neuroblasts per lobe, brains with tll function knocked down contained 4.3 ± 1.2 type II neuroblasts per lobe (n = 10 brains per genotype) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Brains with tll function knocked down contained 4.3 ± 1.2 type II neuroblasts per lobe.
source: Whereas control brains always contained eight type II neuroblasts per lobe, brains with tll function knocked down contained 4.3 ± 1.2 type II neuroblasts per lobe (n = 10 brains per genotype) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: tll mutant neuroblasts showed reduced cell diameters and ectopically expressed Ase.
source: A closer examination revealed that the remaining tll mutant neuroblasts showed reduced cell diameters and ectopically expressed Ase, two characteristics typically associated with INPs in the type II neuroblast lineage (Figure 2A, C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A, C, and D.

claim: tll is required for maintaining type II neuroblasts in an undifferentiated state.
source: This result indicated that tll is required for maintaining type II neuroblasts in an undifferentiated state.
evidence: The claim is based on loss-of-function experiments showing premature differentiation.

claim: Brains with tll misexpressed in INPs contained 150 ± 50 type II neuroblasts per lobe.
source: Brains with tll misexpressed in INPs contained 150 ± 50 type II neuroblasts per lobe, whereas control brains always contained eight type II neuroblasts per lobe (n = 10 brains per genotype) (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Tll misexpression is sufficient to revert INPs to type II neuroblasts.
source: Thus, Tll misexpression is sufficient to revert INPs to type II neuroblasts.
evidence: The claim is based on gain-of-function experiments showing INP reversion.

claim: tll is necessary and sufficient for maintaining type II neuroblasts in an undifferentiated state.
source: These data together led us to conclude that tll is necessary and sufficient for maintaining type II neuroblasts in an undifferentiated state.
evidence: The claim is based on combined loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments.

claim: Sp1::GFP marks type II neuroblasts and most of their progeny that are found exclusively in the dorsal brain region.
source: We found that Sp1::GFP marks type II neuroblasts and most of their progeny that are found exclusively in the dorsal brain region (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Sp1::GFP is detected in some neurons but never in type I neuroblasts in the ventral brain region and in the ventral nerve cord.
source: Sp1::GFP is detected in some neurons but never in type I neuroblasts in the ventral brain region and in the ventral nerve cord (Figure 2I and L).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2I and L.

claim: Sp1::GFP is a new marker for the type II neuroblast lineage.
source: Thus, Sp1::GFP is a new marker for the type II neuroblast lineage (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is based on expression pattern analysis of Sp1::GFP.

claim: The ventral region of control brains contains 29 ± 2.1 type I neuroblasts.
source: While the ventral region of control brains contains 29 ± 2.1 type I neuroblasts, the same region of the brains overexpressing Tll contains 10.6 ± 2.5 type I neuroblasts and hundreds of ectopic type II neuroblasts (n = 10 brains per genotype) (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2I-K.

claim: The ventral region of brains overexpressing Tll contains 10.6 ± 2.5 type I neuroblasts and hundreds of ectopic type II neuroblasts.
source: While the ventral region of control brains contains 29 ± 2.1 type I neuroblasts, the same region of the brains overexpressing Tll contains 10.6 ± 2.5 type I neuroblasts and hundreds of ectopic type II neuroblasts (n = 10 brains per genotype) (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2I-K.

claim: Tll overexpression transforms greater than 60% of type I neuroblasts in the ventral brain region into type II neuroblasts.
source: This result strongly suggests that Tll overexpression transforms greater than 60% of type I neuroblasts in the ventral brain region into type II neuroblasts.
evidence: The claim is based on quantification of neuroblast types before and after Tll overexpression.

claim: Tll overexpression induced hundreds of supernumerary type II neuroblasts in the ventral nerve cord.
source: Similarly, Tll overexpression also induced hundreds of supernumerary type II neuroblasts in the ventral nerve cord (n = 10 brains per genotype) (Figure 2L and M).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2L and M.

claim: Ectopic tll expression is sufficient to molecularly transform type I neuroblasts into type II neuroblasts.
source: Thus, ectopic tll expression is sufficient to molecularly transform type I neuroblasts into type II neuroblasts.
evidence: The claim is based on molecular marker analysis after Tll overexpression.

claim: Erm::V5+ immature INPs were reproducibly observed in the ventral-medial region of the brain overexpressing Tll, but not in the ventral-lateral brain region.
source: We reproducibly observed Erm::V5+ immature INPs in the ventral-medial region of the brain overexpressing Tll, but not in the ventral-lateral brain region (Figure 2O and P).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2O and P.

claim: Progeny of transformed type II neuroblasts in the ventral-medial brain region assume an immature INP identity and then revert into supernumerary type II neuroblasts.
source: This result strongly suggests that progeny of transformed type II neuroblasts in the ventral-medial brain region assume an immature INP identity and then revert into supernumerary type II neuroblasts.
evidence: The claim is based on the presence of Erm::V5+ cells in the ventral-medial region.

claim: Progeny of transformed type II neuroblasts in the ventral-lateral brain region appeared to rapidly revert into supernumerary neuroblasts instead of assuming an immature INP identity.
source: By contrast, progeny of transformed type II neuroblasts in the ventral-lateral brain region appeared to rapidly revert into supernumerary neuroblasts instead of assuming an immature INP identity.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of Erm::V5+ cells in the ventral-lateral region.

claim: tll overexpression is sufficient to molecularly and functionally transform type I neuroblasts into type II neuroblasts.
source: Thus, tll overexpression is sufficient to molecularly and functionally transform type I neuroblasts into type II neuroblasts, and that tll is a master regulator of type II neuroblast functional identity.
evidence: The claim is based on combined molecular and functional analyses of Tll overexpression.

claim: tll is a master regulator of type II neuroblast functional identity.
source: Thus, tll overexpression is sufficient to molecularly and functionally transform type I neuroblasts into type II neuroblasts, and that tll is a master regulator of type II neuroblast functional identity.
evidence: The claim is based on the necessity and sufficiency of tll for type II neuroblast characteristics.

claim: Suppressor of Hairless, the DNA-binding partner of Notch, binds the tll locus in larval brain neuroblasts.
source: A previous study found that Suppressor of Hairless, the DNA-binding partner of Notch, binds the tll locus in larval brain neuroblasts, suggesting that tll is a putative Notch target (Zacharioudaki et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zacharioudaki et al., 2016.

claim: tll is a putative Notch target.
source: A previous study found that Suppressor of Hairless, the DNA-binding partner of Notch, binds the tll locus in larval brain neuroblasts, suggesting that tll is a putative Notch target (Zacharioudaki et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to Zacharioudaki et al., 2016 and inference from binding data.

claim: ermhypo brains display a low frequency of INP reversion to type II neuroblasts.
source: ermhypo brains display a low frequency of INP reversion to type II neuroblasts, and provides a sensitized genetic background for identifying genes required to prevent INP reversion to type II neuroblasts (Janssens et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Janssens et al., 2017.

claim: ermhypo brains contained 31.5 ± 6.8 type II neuroblasts per lobe.
source: We found that ermhypo brains alone contained 31.5 ± 6.8 type II neuroblasts per lobe (n = 10 brains) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Knocking-down ham function with two different UAS-RNAi transgenes reproducibly enhanced the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in ermhypo brains.
source: Although reducing the function of most candidate genes did not enhance the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in ermhypo brains, knocking-down ham function with two different UAS-RNAi transgenes reproducibly enhanced the phenotype (n = 10 brains per transgene) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ham likely plays a role in preventing INPs from reverting to supernumerary type II neuroblasts.
source: Thus, ham likely plays a role in preventing INPs from reverting to supernumerary type II neuroblasts.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic interaction experiments in ermhypo background.

claim: ham is the fly homolog of the vertebrate Prdm16 gene.
source: ham is the fly homolog of the vertebrate Prdm16 gene that encodes a transcription factor and has been shown to play a key role in regulating cell fate decisions in multiple stem cell lineages (Baizabal et al., 2018; Harms et al., 2015; Moore et al., 2002; Shimada et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baizabal et al., 2018; Harms et al., 2015; Moore et al., 2002; Shimada et al., 2017.

claim: Prdm16 has been shown to play a key role in regulating cell fate decisions in multiple stem cell lineages.
source: ham is the fly homolog of the vertebrate Prdm16 gene that encodes a transcription factor and has been shown to play a key role in regulating cell fate decisions in multiple stem cell lineages (Baizabal et al., 2018; Harms et al., 2015; Moore et al., 2002; Shimada et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baizabal et al., 2018; Harms et al., 2015; Moore et al., 2002; Shimada et al., 2017.

claim: A previous study concluded that ham regulates INP proliferation but does not play a role in suppressing supernumerary type II neuroblast formation.
source: A previous study concluded that ham regulates INP proliferation but does not play a role in suppressing supernumerary type II neuroblast formation (Eroglu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eroglu et al., 2014.

claim: The ham1 allele encodes a nearly full-length protein and exhibits similar protein stability as wild-type Ham.
source: The discrepancy between our findings and the published observations might be due to the ham1 allele used in the previous study, which encodes a nearly full-length protein and exhibits similar protein stability as wild-type Ham (Figure 3B; Moore et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3B and citation to Moore et al., 2002.

claim: ham deficiency heterozygous brains reproducibly displayed a mild supernumerary type II neuroblast phenotype (9 ± 0.9 per lobe).
source: First, we examined ham deficiency heterozygous brains and reproducibly observed a mild supernumerary type II neuroblast phenotype (9 ± 0.9 per lobe, n = 12 brains) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Knocking down ham function led to a mild but statistically significant increase in type II neuroblasts per lobe (9.8 ± 1.8) as compared to control brains (8 ± 0).
source: We found that knocking down ham function also led to a mild but statistically significant increase in type II neuroblasts per lobe (9.8 ± 1.8; n = 20 brains) as compared to control brains (8 ± 0; n = 10 brains) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: hamSK1 or hamSK4 homozygous brains show undetectable Ham protein expression.
source: We found that hamSK1 or hamSK4 homozygous brains show undetectable Ham protein expression (Figure 3C and D; data not presented).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Mutant Ham protein encoded by the hamSK1 or hamSK4 allele is unstable.
source: This result strongly suggests that mutant Ham protein encoded by the hamSK1 or hamSK4 allele is unstable, and that these two new ham alleles are strongly loss-of-function mutants.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of detectable Ham protein in mutant brains.

claim: hamSK1 and hamSK4 alleles are strongly loss-of-function mutants.
source: This result strongly suggests that mutant Ham protein encoded by the hamSK1 or hamSK4 allele is unstable, and that these two new ham alleles are strongly loss-of-function mutants.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of detectable Ham protein in mutant brains.

claim: hamSK1 homozygous brains contained 40 ± 10 type II neuroblasts per lobe.
source: Indeed, hamSK1 homozygous brains contained 40 ± 10 type II neuroblasts per lobe (n = 15 brains) (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Ham is detectable in Ase+ immature INPs and remains expressed in all INPs.
source: Because Ham is detectable in Ase+ immature INPs and remains expressed in all INPs (Eroglu et al., 2014), we conclude that ham is a novel regulator of INP commitment.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eroglu et al., 2014.

claim: ham is a novel regulator of INP commitment.
source: Because Ham is detectable in Ase+ immature INPs and remains expressed in all INPs (Eroglu et al., 2014), we conclude that ham is a novel regulator of INP commitment.
evidence: The claim is based on expression pattern and loss-of-function phenotype.

claim: The heterozygosity of erm did not increase total type II neuroblasts (8.1 ± 0.3 per lobe).
source: Although the heterozygosity of erm did not increase total type II neuroblasts (8.1 ± 0.3 per lobe; n = 11 brains), it enhanced the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in ham deficiency heterozygous brains and in hamSK1 homozygous brains (14 ± 2.2 vs. 76.2 ± 18.3 type II neuroblasts per lobe; n = 14 brains per genotype) (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: The heterozygosity of erm enhanced the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in ham deficiency heterozygous brains and in hamSK1 homozygous brains (14 ± 2.2 vs. 76.2 ± 18.3 type II neuroblasts per lobe).
source: Although the heterozygosity of erm did not increase total type II neuroblasts (8.1 ± 0.3 per lobe; n = 11 brains), it enhanced the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in ham deficiency heterozygous brains and in hamSK1 homozygous brains (14 ± 2.2 vs. 76.2 ± 18.3 type II neuroblasts per lobe; n = 14 brains per genotype) (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: Ham functions synergistically with Erm to suppress supernumerary type II neuroblast formation.
source: We conclude that Ham functions synergistically with Erm to suppress supernumerary type II neuroblast formation.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic interaction experiments showing enhanced phenotype in double mutants.

claim: Re-activation of Notch signaling in INPs drives supernumerary type II neuroblast formation in erm-null brains.
source: Re-activation of Notch signaling in INPs drives supernumerary type II neuroblast formation in erm-null brains (Weng et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Weng et al., 2010.

claim: erm,ham heterozygous brains contained 12.7 ± 1.6 type II neuroblasts per lobe.
source: Whereas erm,ham heterozygous brains alone contained 12.7 ± 1.6 type II neuroblasts per lobe (n = 9 brains), overexpressing ham in INPs driven by Erm-Gal4(III) rescued the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in erm,ham double heterozygous brains (8.2 ± 0.8 type II neuroblasts per lobe; n = 24 brains) (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Overexpressing ham in INPs rescued the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in erm,ham double heterozygous brains (8.2 ± 0.8 type II neuroblasts per lobe).
source: Whereas erm,ham heterozygous brains alone contained 12.7 ± 1.6 type II neuroblasts per lobe (n = 9 brains), overexpressing ham in INPs driven by Erm-Gal4(III) rescued the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in erm,ham double heterozygous brains (8.2 ± 0.8 type II neuroblasts per lobe; n = 24 brains) (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Supernumerary type II neuroblasts originate from INPs in ham-null brains.
source: This result strongly suggests that supernumerary type II neuroblasts originate from INPs in ham-null brains.
evidence: The claim is based on rescue experiments showing that Ham expression in INPs suppresses the phenotype.

claim: In wild-type clones, the parental type II neuroblast was always surrounded by Ase- and Ase+ immature INPs.
source: In wild-type clones (n = 9 clones), the parental type II neuroblast was always surrounded by Ase- and Ase+ immature INPs (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Supernumerary neuroblasts in hamSK1 homozygous clones (2.5 ± 1.7 type II neuroblasts per clone) were always located far away from parental neuroblasts and surrounded by Ase+ cells.
source: By contrast, supernumerary neuroblasts in hamSK1 homozygous clones (2.5 ± 1.7 type II neuroblasts per clone; n = 11 clones) were always located far away from parental neuroblasts and surrounded by Ase+ cells that were most likely Ase+ immature INPs and ganglion mother cells (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: It is highly unlikely that supernumerary neuroblasts in hamSK1 homozygous clones originated from symmetric neuroblast division based on their location relative to parental neuroblasts and the cell types that surround them.
source: It is highly unlikely that supernumerary neuroblasts in hamSK1 homozygous clones originated from symmetric neuroblast division based on their location relative to parental neuroblasts and the cell types that surround them.
evidence: The claim is based on spatial analysis of supernumerary neuroblasts in clones.

claim: Ham suppresses INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts.
source: Thus, we conclude that Ham suppresses INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts.
evidence: The claim is based on clonal analysis showing supernumerary neuroblasts arise from INPs.

claim: Mis-expressing HamΔC-ZF triggered premature differentiation in type II neuroblasts, identical to mis-expression of full-length Ham.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, mis-expressing HamΔC-ZF triggered premature differentiation in type II neuroblasts, identical to mis-expression of full-length Ham (n = 10 brains per genotype) (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Overexpressing HamΔC-ZF rescued the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in hamSK1 homozygous brains to a similar extent as overexpressing full-length Ham (11.1 ± 1.4 vs. 11.9 ± 1.3 type II neuroblasts per lobe).
source: Overexpressing HamΔC-ZF rescued the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in hamSK1 homozygous brains to a similar extent as overexpressing full-length Ham (11.1 ± 1.4 vs. 11.9 ± 1.3 type II neuroblasts per lobe; n = 11 or 9 brains, respectively) (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Overexpressing ERD::HamN-ZF rescued the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in hamSK1 homozygous brains (14 ± 2.3 type II neuroblasts per lobe).
source: Under identical conditions, overexpressing a constitutive transcriptional repressor form of Ham containing only the N-terminal zinc fingers (ERD::HamN-ZF) also rescued the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in hamSK1 homozygous brains (14 ± 2.3 type II neuroblasts per lobe; n = 9 brains) (Figure 4D and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D and F.

claim: Ham functions through the N-terminal zinc finger to repress the transcription of genes that can trigger INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts.
source: These results indicate that Ham functions through the N-terminal zinc finger to repress the transcription of genes that can trigger INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts.
evidence: The claim is based on rescue experiments with truncated Ham proteins.

claim: VP16::HamN-ZF misexpression in type II neuroblasts was sufficient to induce supernumerary neuroblast formation (17.1 ± 4.7 type II neuroblasts per lobe).
source: We found that VP16::HamN-ZF misexpression in type II neuroblasts was sufficient to induce supernumerary neuroblast formation (17.1 ± 4.7 type II neuroblasts per lobe; n = 10 brains) (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Ham suppresses INP reversion by recognizing target genes through its N-terminal zinc-finger motif and repressing their transcription.
source: Because VP16::HamN-ZF can exert a dominant-negative effect, we conclude that Ham suppresses INP reversion by recognizing target genes through its N-terminal zinc-finger motif and repressing their transcription.
evidence: The claim is based on the dominant-negative effect of VP16::HamN-ZF.

claim: tll heterozygous brains contained 8.2 ± 0.4 type II neuroblasts per lobe.
source: tll heterozygous brains contained 8.2 ± 0.4 type II neuroblasts per lobe, whereas erm,ham double heterozygous brains contained 11 ± 1.2 type II neuroblasts per lobe (n = 10 or 25 brains, respectively) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: erm,ham double heterozygous brains contained 11 ± 1.2 type II neuroblasts per lobe.
source: tll heterozygous brains contained 8.2 ± 0.4 type II neuroblasts per lobe, whereas erm,ham double heterozygous brains contained 11 ± 1.2 type II neuroblasts per lobe (n = 10 or 25 brains, respectively) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The heterozygosity of tll consistently suppressed the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in erm,ham double heterozygous brains (8.4 ± 0.6 type II neuroblasts per lobe).
source: The heterozygosity of tll consistently suppressed the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in erm,ham double heterozygous brains (8.4 ± 0.6 type II neuroblasts per lobe; n = 22 brains) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Erm and Ham inactivate tll during INP commitment.
source: This result strongly supports our hypothesis that Erm and Ham inactivate tll during INP commitment.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic suppression experiments.

claim: Tll::GFP becomes ectopically expressed in INPs in erm,ham double heterozygous brains.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, we found that Tll::GFP becomes ectopically expressed in INPs in erm,ham double heterozygous brains (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Small cells expressing Tll::GFP and Deadpan (Dpn) but not Ase were reproducibly observed in erm,ham double heterozygous brains, which were most likely supernumerary type II neuroblasts newly derived from INP reversion.
source: In these brains, we reproducibly observed small cells expressing Tll::GFP and Deadpan (Dpn) but not Ase that were most likely supernumerary type II neuroblasts newly derived from INP reversion (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: One copy of the tll::GFP(BAC) transgene mildly enhanced the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in erm,ham double heterozygous brains (15.4 ± 1.8 vs. 11.1 ± 1 type II neuroblasts per lobe).
source: Furthermore, we found that one copy of the tll::GFP(BAC) transgene mildly enhanced the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in erm,ham double heterozygous brains (15.4 ± 1.8 vs. 11.1 ± 1 type II neuroblasts per lobe; n = 12 or 11 brains, respectively) (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Tll::GFP expression in type II neuroblasts overexpressing Erm was mildly reduced prior to upregulation of Ase expression, and declined further following upregulation of Ase expression.
source: We found that Tll::GFP expression in type II neuroblasts overexpressing Erm was mildly reduced prior to upregulation of Ase expression, and declined further following upregulation of Ase expression (Figure 5F, G and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5F, G, and I.

claim: Tll::GFP expression in type II neuroblasts overexpressing Ham was unaffected prior to upregulation of Ase expression, but rapidly declined following upregulation of Ase expression.
source: By contrast, Tll::GFP expression in type II neuroblasts overexpressing Ham was unaffected prior to upregulation of Ase expression, but rapidly declined following upregulation of Ase expression (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5H and I.

claim: Sequential inactivation by Erm and Ham during INP commitment renders tll refractory to activation in INPs.
source: Together, these data strongly support our model that sequential inactivation by Erm and Ham during INP commitment renders tll refractory to activation in INPs.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis of Tll::GFP expression upon Erm or Ham overexpression.

claim: Knock-down of Notch function in INPs had no effect on type II neuroblasts in wild-type brains (7.9 ± 0.3 type II neuroblasts per lobe).
source: Knock-down of Notch function in INPs had no effect on type II neuroblasts in wild-type brains (7.9 ± 0.3 type II neuroblasts per lobe; n = 17 brains) (Figure 5J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: In hamSK1 homozygous brains, knocking-down Notch function in INPs reduced the number of type II neuroblasts per lobe from 128 ± 39.6 to 36.4 ± 11.6.
source: However, in hamSK1 homozygous brains, knocking-down Notch function in INPs reduced the number of type II neuroblasts per lobe from 128 ± 39.6 to 36.4 ± 11.6 (n = 9 brains per genotype) (Figure 5J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Re-activation of Notch signaling triggers INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts in ham-null brains.
source: This result indicates that re-activation of Notch signaling triggers INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts in ham-null brains.
evidence: The claim is based on Notch knockdown experiments in ham-null background.

claim: Overexpressing Notchintra induced a drastically more severe supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in erm,ham double heterozygous brains (3,437.6 ± 586.8 type II neuroblasts per lobe) than in erm or ham single heterozygous brains (687 ± 134.3 vs. 588.6 ± 77.6 type II neuroblasts per lobe).
source: Consistently, overexpressing constitutively activated Notch (Notchintra) induced a drastically more severe supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in erm,ham double heterozygous brains (3,437.6 ± 586.8 type II neuroblasts per lobe; n = 9 brains) than in erm or ham single heterozygous brains (687 ± 134.3 vs. 588.6 ± 77.6 type II neuroblasts per lobe; n = 9 or 11 brains, respectively) (Figure 5K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Inactivation by Erm and Ham during INP commitment renders tll refractory to Notch signaling in INPs.
source: Thus, we propose that inactivation by Erm and Ham during INP commitment renders tll refractory to Notch signaling in INPs (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on genetic experiments showing synergistic effects of erm and ham mutations with Notch activation.

claim: erm-null brains contained 1824.6 ± 520.7 type II neuroblasts per lobe.
source: erm-null brains alone contained 1824.6 ± 520.7 type II neuroblasts per lobe (n = 13 brains) (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overexpressing full-length Ham or HamΔC-ZF strongly suppressed the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in erm-null brains (34.5 ± 8.3 vs. 64.6 ± 18.3 neuroblasts per lobe).
source: Overexpressing full-length Ham or HamΔC-ZF strongly suppressed the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in erm-null brains (34.5 ± 8.3 vs. 64.6 ± 18.3 neuroblasts per lobe; n = 13 or 7 brains, respectively) (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ham over-expression can replace endogenous Erm function to suppress INP reversion.
source: This result indicates that Ham over-expression can replace endogenous Erm function to suppress INP reversion, suggesting that these two transcriptional repressors function through an identical chromatin-modifying protein to inactivate tll during INP commitment.
evidence: The claim is based on rescue experiments in erm-null background.

claim: Erm and Ham function through an identical chromatin-modifying protein to inactivate tll during INP commitment.
source: This result indicates that Ham over-expression can replace endogenous Erm function to suppress INP reversion, suggesting that these two transcriptional repressors function through an identical chromatin-modifying protein to inactivate tll during INP commitment.
evidence: The claim is based on the ability of Ham to substitute for Erm function.

claim: Reducing the activity of PRC2 or heterochromatin protein 1, as well as decreasing the recruitment of Heterochromatin Protein 1, had no effect on the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in ham heterozygous brains.
source: Reducing the activity of PRC2 or heterochromatin protein 1, as well as decreasing the recruitment of Heterochromatin Protein 1, had no effect on the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in ham heterozygous brains (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Reducing the activity of nucleosome remodelers alone led to a mild supernumerary type II neuroblast phenotype, but did not further enhance the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in ham heterozygous brains.
source: While reducing the activity of nucleosome remodelers alone led to a mild supernumerary type II neuroblast phenotype, it did not further enhance the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in ham heterozygous brains (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Reducing the activity of histone deacetylase 3 (Hdac3) alone resulted in a mild supernumerary type II neuroblast phenotype and significantly enhanced the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in ham heterozygous brains.
source: By contrast, reducing the activity of histone deacetylase 3 (Hdac3) alone resulted in a mild supernumerary type II neuroblast phenotype and significantly enhanced the supernumerary neuroblast phenotype in ham heterozygous brains (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ham likely functions through Hdac3 to prevent INP reversion.
source: These results led us to conclude that Ham likely functions through Hdac3 to prevent INP reversion.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic interaction experiments between ham and hdac3.

claim: erm heterozygous brains alone did not display a supernumerary type II neuroblast phenotype.
source: erm heterozygous brains alone did not display a supernumerary type II neuroblast phenotype (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Knocking-down hdac3 function in erm heterozygous brains led to a more than three-fold increase in supernumerary type II neuroblasts as compared to wild-type brains.
source: Knocking-down hdac3 function in erm heterozygous brains led to a more than three-fold increase in supernumerary type II neuroblasts as compared to wild-type brains (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Hdac3 functions together with Erm and Ham to silence tll during INP commitment.
source: These data strongly support a model that Hdac3 functions together with Erm and Ham to silence tll during INP commitment.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic interaction experiments between hdac3 and erm or ham.

claim: Knock down of hdac3 function in type II neuroblasts led to ectopic Tll::GFP expression in immature INPs and INPs.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, knock down of hdac3 function in type II neuroblasts and their progeny led to ectopic Tll::GFP expression in immature INPs and INPs (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6E-G.

claim: Hdac3 is required for inactivating tll during INP commitment.
source: These results confirmed that Hdac3 is required for inactivating tll during INP commitment.
evidence: The claim is based on ectopic Tll::GFP expression upon hdac3 knockdown.

claim: Erm and Ham likely function through Hdac3 to prevent INP from reverting to supernumerary type II neuroblasts by continually inactivating tll.
source: Thus, we conclude that Erm and Ham likely function through Hdac3 to prevent INP from reverting to supernumerary type II neuroblasts by continually inactivating tll.
evidence: The claim is based on combined genetic and molecular evidence linking Erm, Ham, Hdac3, and tll.

claim: The expansion of OSVZ neural stem cells drives the evolution of lissencephalic brains to gyrencephalic brains.
source: The expansion of OSVZ neural stem cells, which indirectly produce neurons by initially generating intermediate progenitors, drives the evolution of lissencephalic brains to gyrencephalic brains (Cárdenas and Borrell, 2020; Delaunay et al., 2017; Di Lullo and Kriegstein, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cárdenas and Borrell, 2020; Delaunay et al., 2017; Di Lullo and Kriegstein, 2017.

claim: Tll is necessary and sufficient for the maintenance of an undifferentiated state and the competency to generate intermediate progenitors in type II neuroblasts.
source: In this study, we have provided compelling evidence demonstrating that Tll is necessary and sufficient for the maintenance of an undifferentiated state and the competency to generate intermediate progenitors in type II neuroblasts (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Two sequentially activated transcriptional repressors, Erm and Ham, likely function through Hdac3 to silence tll during INP commitment ensuring normal indirect neurogenesis in larval brains.
source: We also showed that two sequentially activated transcriptional repressors, Erm and Ham, likely function through Hdac3 to silence tll during INP commitment ensuring normal indirect neurogenesis in larval brains.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Continual inactivation of stem cell functional identity genes by histone deacetylation allows intermediate progenitors to stably commit to generating sufficient and diverse differentiated cells during neurogenesis.
source: We propose that continual inactivation of stem cell functional identity genes by histone deacetylation allows intermediate progenitors to stably commit to generating sufficient and diverse differentiated cells during neurogenesis.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the findings of the study.

claim: Overexpressing Notchintra or the downstream transcriptional repressors Dpn, E(spl)mγ, and Klumpfuss (Klu) induces the formation of supernumerary type II neuroblasts at the expense of generating immature INPs via the inhibition of erm activation.
source: In the fly type II neuroblast lineage, overexpressing Notchintra or the downstream transcriptional repressors Dpn, E(spl)mγ, and Klumpfuss (Klu) induces the formation of supernumerary type II neuroblasts at the expense of generating immature INPs via the inhibition of erm activation (Janssens et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Janssens et al., 2017.

claim: The Notch-Dpn/E(spl)mγ/Klu axis provides an evolutionarily conserved mechanism to maintain neural stem cells in an undifferentiated state.
source: These results indicate that the Notch-Dpn/E(spl)mγ/Klu axis provides an evolutionarily conserved mechanism to maintain neural stem cells in an undifferentiated state.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental results and evolutionary conservation.

claim: Overexpressing Notchintra but not Dpn, E(spl)mγ, and Klu in combination in INPs is sufficient to drive supernumerary type II neuroblast formation.
source: Although overexpressing Notchintra but not Dpn, E(spl)mγ, and Klu in combination in INPs is sufficient to drive supernumerary type II neuroblast formation, Notchintra overexpression is not sufficient to transform a type I neuroblast into a type II neuroblast (data not presented).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Notchintra overexpression is not sufficient to transform a type I neuroblast into a type II neuroblast.
source: Although overexpressing Notchintra but not Dpn, E(spl)mγ, and Klu in combination in INPs is sufficient to drive supernumerary type II neuroblast formation, Notchintra overexpression is not sufficient to transform a type I neuroblast into a type II neuroblast (data not presented).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Notch functions as a general activator of genes expression in type II neuroblasts.
source: Thus, we propose that Notch functions as a general activator of genes expression in type II neuroblasts, and specific regulators of type II neuroblast functional identities must exist.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on experimental observations.

claim: ChIP-seq on fly embryonic nuclear extract using the Tll::GFP(Bac) transgenic protein identified hundreds of putative Tll target genes that include all previously characterized regulators of type II neuroblast functional identities.
source: ChIP-seq on fly embryonic nuclear extract using the Tll::GFP(Bac) transgenic protein identified hundreds of putative Tll target genes that include all previously characterized regulators of type II neuroblast functional identities (Davis et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Davis et al., 2018.

claim: Tll binds dpn, E(spl)mγ and klu loci in embryos.
source: Tll binds dpn, E(spl)mγ and klu loci in embryos, suggesting that Tll likely regulates their expression.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data from Davis et al., 2018.

claim: Tll likely regulates dpn, E(spl)mγ and klu expression.
source: Tll binds dpn, E(spl)mγ and klu loci in embryos, suggesting that Tll likely regulates their expression.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from ChIP-seq binding data.

claim: The vertebrate homolog of Tll, Tlx, has been shown to function as a transcriptional activator during neurogenesis.
source: The vertebrate homolog of Tll, Tlx, has been shown to function as a transcriptional activator during neurogenesis (Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2017.

claim: Tll might maintain type II neuroblasts in an undifferentiated state by promoting dpn, E(spl)mγ and klu expression.
source: Thus, Tll might maintain type II neuroblasts in an undifferentiated state by promoting dpn, E(spl)mγ and klu expression.
evidence: The claim is a speculative model based on binding data and functional homology.

claim: Tll also binds pntP1 and btd loci in embryos.
source: Tll also binds pntP1 and btd loci in embryos.
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-seq data from Davis et al., 2018.

claim: Mis-expression of PntP1 or Btd can transform type I neuroblasts in the ventral brain region into type II neuroblasts.
source: Similar to Tll overexpression, mis-expression of PntP1 or Btd can transform type I neuroblasts in the ventral brain region into type II neuroblasts (Komori et al., 2014b; Xie et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Komori et al., 2014b; Xie et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2011.

claim: It is plausible that tll functions through pntP1 or btd to regulate the competency to generate INPs in type II neuroblasts.
source: Thus, it is plausible that tll functions through pntP1 or btd to regulate the competency to generate INPs in type II neuroblasts.
evidence: The claim is a speculative model based on binding data and functional similarities.

claim: Tll is key component of the regulatory mechanism that endows type II neuroblasts with lineage-specific functional identities.
source: These results strongly support our model that Tll is key component of the regulatory mechanism that endows type II neuroblasts with lineage-specific functional identities.
evidence: The claim is based on combined experimental and ChIP-seq evidence.

claim: Prdm16 contains two separately defined zinc-finger motifs, with each likely recognizing unique target genes.
source: Prdm16 contains two separately defined zinc-finger motifs, with each likely recognizing unique target genes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Prdm16 protein structure.

claim: Prdm16 can function through a variety of cofactors to activate or repress target gene expression, independent of its DNA-binding capacity.
source: Prdm16 can also function through a variety of cofactors to activate or repress target gene expression, independent of its DNA-binding capacity.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Prdm16 function.

claim: The N-terminal zinc-finger motif is required for Ham function in immature INPs.
source: By using a combination of previously isolated alleles and new protein-null alleles, we demonstrated that the N-terminal zinc-finger motif is required for Ham function in immature INPs.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic experiments with different ham alleles.

claim: Ham prevents INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts by recognizing target genes via the N-terminal zinc-finger motif and possibly repressing their transcription.
source: Based on the overexpression of a series of chimeric proteins containing the N-terminal zinc-finger motif, our data indicate that Ham prevents INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts by recognizing target genes via the N-terminal zinc-finger motif and possibly repressing their transcription.
evidence: The claim is based on experiments with chimeric Ham proteins.

claim: INP commitment lasts approximately 6–8 hr following the generation of an immature INP.
source: INP commitment lasts approximately 6–8 hr following the generation of an immature INP (Berger et al., 2012; Homem et al., 2014); after this time, the immature INP transitions into an INP.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Berger et al., 2012; Homem et al., 2014.

claim: erm is poised for activation in type II neuroblasts and becomes rapidly activated in the newly generated immature INP less than 90 min after its generation.
source: erm is poised for activation in type II neuroblasts and becomes rapidly activated in the newly generated immature INP less than 90 min after its generation (Janssens et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Janssens et al., 2017.

claim: Erm-mediated transcriptional repression allows for the rapid inactivation of type II neuroblast functional identity genes.
source: As such, Erm-mediated transcriptional repression allows for the rapid inactivation of type II neuroblast functional identity genes.
evidence: The claim is based on the rapid activation of Erm and its repressor function.

claim: Erm expression rapidly declines in INPs when Notch signaling becomes reactivated.
source: Because Erm expression rapidly declines in INPs when Notch signaling becomes reactivated, a second transcriptional repressor that becomes activated after Erm and whose expression is maintained throughout the life of an INP is required to continually inactivate type II neuroblast functional identity genes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Erm expression dynamics.

claim: Ham becomes expressed in immature INPs 3–4 hr after the onset of Erm expression and is detected in all INPs.
source: Ham is an excellent candidate because it becomes expressed in immature INPs 3–4 hr after the onset of Erm expression and is detected in all INPs.
evidence: The claim is based on expression analysis of Ham.

claim: ham functions synergistically with erm to prevent INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts.
source: Furthermore, ham functions synergistically with erm to prevent INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts, and overexpressed Ham can partially substitute for endogenous Erm.
evidence: The claim is based on genetic interaction experiments.

claim: Overexpressed Ham can partially substitute for endogenous Erm.
source: Furthermore, ham functions synergistically with erm to prevent INP reversion to supernumerary type II neuroblasts, and overexpressed Ham can partially substitute for endogenous Erm.
evidence: The claim is based on rescue experiments in erm-null background.

claim: Erm- and Ham-mediated transcriptional repression renders type II neuroblast functional identity genes refractory to activation by Notch signaling throughout the lifespan of the INP.
source: Thus, Erm- and Ham-mediated transcriptional repression renders type II neuroblast functional identity genes refractory to activation by Notch signaling throughout the lifespan of the INP, ensuring the generation of differentiated cell types rather than supernumerary type II neuroblasts instead.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the sequential action of Erm and Ham.

claim: Blocking apoptosis in lineage clones derived from PRC2-mutant type II neuroblasts did not lead to supernumerary neuroblast formation.
source: Our finding is consistent with a recent study showing that blocking apoptosis in lineage clones derived from PRC2-mutant type II neuroblasts did not lead to supernumerary neuroblast formation (Abdusselamoglu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Abdusselamoglu et al., 2019.

claim: Genes specifying type II neuroblast functional identity, such as tll, are likely silenced rather than decommissioned in INPs.
source: Our data strongly suggest that genes specifying type II neuroblast functional identity, such as tll, are likely silenced rather than decommissioned in INPs.
evidence: The claim is based on the ability of Notch to reactivate tll in INPs lacking Erm and Ham.

claim: Continual histone deacetylation is required to counter the transcriptional activator activity of endogenous Notch and silence tll in INPs.
source: We speculate that continual histone deacetylation is required to counter the transcriptional activator activity of endogenous Notch and silence tll in INPs (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is a speculative model based on the role of Hdac3 in tll silencing.

claim: The chromatin in the tll locus might be close and inaccessible to the Notch transcriptional activator complex in type I neuroblasts.
source: By contrast, the chromatin in the tll locus might be close and inaccessible to the Notch transcriptional activator complex in type I neuroblasts; thus, overexpressing Notchintra cannot transform type I neuroblasts into type II neuroblasts.
evidence: The claim is a speculative model to explain differential Notch responsiveness.
